Looking at this document, and you're talking about the established procedures, this is an order that's issued by Mr. Zarko Tole, dated the 4th of September, 1993, and what he's ordering is that on the following day, the 5th of September, movements of UN, UNHCR, and UNPROFOR at the military police check-points in your area of responsibility, especially toward Vranica, saying: "Stop them, stop all movements, and all movements towards Jablanica is to be prevented. These activities are to be carried out until 1500 hours. And then he continues at point number 2: "It is to be done so as to appear as self-willedness of policemen at the check-points and as if we were doing everything to let them through." Item 3: "After 1500 hours, allow further movements as if nothing happened." Is this a practice that you encountered in your capacity as the deputy and then the head of the ODPR, convoys being held up at check-points for reasons that aren't clear? Perhaps you thought the arrangements had been made, and then all of a sudden things don't actually work out the way you had hoped?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: That was absolutely not the practice. I see this document for the first time. And after three hours on that same day, passage was allowed, we see from this document, the Court was also able to see how much aid and how many convoys passed through within a short period of time and how much aid arrived with the assistance of the Office for Refugees and Displaced Persons. This was the largest quantity that came along ground routes, and we received a great deal of gratitude for this. I'm not saying that occasionally these convoys were not held up, because we know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The document that you looked at yesterday, I believe, on -- that listed all the convoys was 3D 00921, and we've given you a copy of that. It's in the Defence binder, but we have additional copies to --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is the -- this is the sheet that has all the listings, and I'm just very briefly, my only real question on this, Mr. Raguz, was -- and it was noted by the President, actually, that going through this, you'll see a lot of convoys going to Zenica and Sarajevo, and I'm looking at the month of September 1993, October 1993. There are some convoys, I'm seeing, going into Bugojno in this period, Jablanica, Tuzla. There's one to Kakanj on the 10th of October, 1993. And this continues on. We're seeing on page -- the ERN number is 0365-3937, there are convoys in here to Mostar. But, again, as was pointed out, a lot of convoys to Sarajevo and Zenica. And then at the page that ends with the digits 3938, the tally comes to an end on the 2nd of December, 1993. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then if you turn the page, it starts -- it's -- we go back to June, it appears, and then we see a lot of other convoys, and these are going to places like Grude, Citluk, Mostar, Posusje, Prozor, Bugojno, and again as we go through these pages, it seems to me that there are a greater number of convoys here that are going to places within Western Herzegovina or the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which you -- would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: No, because you have collective information here on the amount of aid that was transported to areas under the control of the Armija and of the HVO. The information is very precise, because each request included certain things. I have to finish my answer, because you asked me about this, and this is what I want to say. Through these convoys that the ODPR dealt with, over two-thirds of the aid went to Sarajevo, Zenica, and other areas under the control of the ABiH, and they passed through areas under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it --

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: All the convoys are on record. That's a good thing. And that remains so for posterity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is it possible that it was the relief organisations that are indicated here that were making their determinations as to where aid was needed the most? In other words, is it possible that aid was needed more in Zenica or Sarajevo and it was perhaps needed less at the time in Ljubuski or Medjugorje, for example, where there was no significant military activity during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: When explaining the procedure for the convoys that had passed through, I had already said that humanitarian organisations autonomously decided on the final destination for the delivery of aid, and I said that this was their responsibility. We never told them to deliver it to one destination, not to another. We had no individual requests to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The last exhibit and the last question, Mr. Raguz, is P 03394. It's in binder number 1. During your direct examination, you referred to a report on the work of the ODPR. I think the one you referred to on direct was a different one, but I just have one question about this one. This one's dated the 12th of July, 1993, so it's early during the time of your association with ODPR?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And it's not numbered, or at least the version I have is not numbered, so I'll try to just walk you through to the part I'm interested in. I'm looking at the bottom of page 2 of the English version, where it begins: "On March 11, 1993, the rules of the internal structure and method of work of the office were adopted." Do you see that, Mr. Raguz?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I'm looking for that, Mr. Prosecutor. On the second page --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It may be -- it begins with the words: "On 11 March ..."

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: It's the first page in my version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay, all right. And is that a reference to the rules on the work of the ODPR that were made by Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Probably, the rules of the internal organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Okay. And then moving forward, the next paragraph says -- starts off with the words: "Having set up an analysis department at the end of March ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Which page is that? Page 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's probably page 2 for you: "Having set up an analysis department --"

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We're still not quite yet to the part I want to ask you about, but this is the best way to bring you there. The next paragraph begins with the words: "Before the department for the collection distribution and selection of humanitarian aid (mid-March 1993)." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph begins with the words: "One of the greatest problems that this department has faced has been the problem of shipping aid (through a lack of funds) --"

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: " ... [Previous translation continues]... difficulties in the convoys and the shipments." The next paragraph begins with the discussion of -- it says: "At this office's initiative, a decision on controlling the influx of humanitarian aid in HZ-HB was adopted." Do you see that? Okay. And then finally it brings us to the paragraph I wanted to ask you about. It says: "This office has established good cooperation with the HVO Main Staff logistics in Grude, and we donated to them substantial amounts of various items, and we organised joint convoys for Central Bosnia and other hazardous areas (example: the last convoy to Konjic and Zepce)." The question is this, Mr. Raguz, was it ODPR's policy to donate humanitarian goods or any of the goods that it had for distribution to refugees and displaced persons, did it donate those types of goods, in fact, to the HVO Main Staff, or do you know?

utterances.speaker: MARTIN RAGUZ
utterances.text: This was at the beginning of my arrival. I said that I had established quite clear procedures, transparent procedures, and I don't think that we can say that these were the general policies. I wouldn't exclude such cases, but while I was there, it wasn't a policy, nor did anyone ask me to pursue such a policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, you have now completed your cross-examination. As far as Mr. Karnavas' request is concerned, is there anything you would like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. In light of what was covered on cross-examination and the direct examination, we feel that you could not benefit any more from any redirect, so there will not be any redirect examination. And we want to thank Mr. Raguz for coming here and giving his evidence, and we wish him the best of luck and a safe trip back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Stringer, you said that you would answer Mr. Karnavas' question about the investigations into the witness. I give you the floor if you want to answer that question. It's for you to decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I can look into it, if Your Honour -- or if the Trial Chamber wishes me to do so. I don't have a ready answer at this point. We certainly don't have a policy of -- along the lines as has been suggested, and certainly it's not our policy to do anything to discourage people from coming. You know, on the other hand, I think it's clear, and I can say this, any witness who comes here, we are interested to know if any witness has a criminal background. It's a very normal, at least where I come from, practice to try to ascertain whether a person, a witness, has a criminal background, because that's a factor that can affect their credibility as a witness. And so if a background check has been requested on that basis, it's quite possible that that's taken place. But, again, I think it's part of a normal procedure on checking about a witness to see whether there's a crime in his background that would affect his credibility as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't quite answer my question. Are background checks being made? It seems like we're waffling here. I find it incredibly difficult to swallow that the senior trial lawyer in this case would not know whether background checks were requested of all the Defence witnesses. I know for a fact that our very first witness was checked, and it seems that it's not just asking the local authorities whether they have on their computer something, but engaging -- it would appear that part of this process are secret services being engaged to snooping around. And I think this has serious implications concerning some of our witnesses, because if you have a situation, as you have today in Bosnia-Herzegovina, where still, albeit peaceful, it is precarious and politics there is somewhat of a blood sport, I think that these sorts of checks by secret agencies tend to have a chilling effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I've listened carefully to what you have said, and it's quite logical that when a witness appears, the Prosecution checks to see whether he has a criminal record, and he then asks the local OTP whether Mr. X had a criminal past, had anything to do with the police or the legal system. There's nothing to object there. But Mr. Karnavas has raised another matter that I have just found out about. Has the OTP launched an investigation into the gentleman's past, that concerns all the aspects of his past, fiscal past, private/political past; were the secret services involved in this? So this is the issue that Mr. Karnavas has raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No, that's absolutely not correct, Mr. President. It's the practice with every witness, whatever country they come from. So with this witness, if he's coming from Bosnia-Herzegovina, we -- the normal course, because I can't say for sure what is the specific procedure that was used here, I can tell you the normal course would be to request of Federation authorities to check to see whether any given witness has a criminal record. In addition to that, of course, we do things like Google searches, and that's how we found Mr. Raguz' CV on the internet on the European Parliament web site. So we absolutely check witnesses. We do it ourselves, and we also make requests of the national authorities who have access to the relevant information on criminal background. There is certainly no intention or request to do anything more in terms of prying or inquiring into the private lives of witnesses. I think Mr. Karnavas has so far managed to assemble a quite impressive array of witnesses to come here as part of his case in chief. I'm surprised to hear if there's been any chilling, because actually virtually all of the people that he's called have been rather high profile and well known. And so we check criminal backgrounds. We do it by requesting assistance from national authorities, which is our right to do and which is the procedure that's provided under the Statute of the Tribunal, and I want to assure the Trial Chamber, Mr. Karnavas, as well as the witness himself that there is no intention on the part of the Prosecution to cross the line or make any effort to do anything that goes beyond the normal type of investigation that would be done for any witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Nozica first of all.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was waiting to see whether Mr. Karnavas would address this issue. As he hasn't, I would like to add something that's very important. We have no reason to believe the Prosecution is working in the way described, that he requests information for witnesses that might have to do with a possible criminal record, but I would like to point out the danger of such requests. When such requests arrive, when the state organs and certain services in Bosnia-Herzegovina receive such requests, they can be abused by those services. I believe that this is a problem that occurred in the case of this witness. Unfortunately, Bosnia and Herzegovina is still nationally divided, and perhaps it's even worse, but it's more sophisticated. When this request comes for the Defence witness in the Prlic case, it can be abused by the secret services under the control of the Bosniak side, perhaps, and in such cases investigations can be conducted, and these investigations result in scaring the witnesses or discouraging the witnesses, or perhaps discouraging them from testifying here about things they are familiar with. I didn't say this just to inform the Chamber about the fact, but also because I believe that it would be good if, when the Prosecution makes such requests, it also informs the extent to which they are asking for information, the scope of their requests, so that they do not abuse the Prosecution request and act in a way that might be detrimental to this Tribunal and to this case. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you are on your feet. Is this because you want to spend your ten minutes on saying something or do you want to react to what has just been said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to react to what has been said, because I know of an investigation conducted by the special services in my case, but I would like the following question to be put to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is done correctly, then it's a written request to the bodies concerned, please do such-and-such a thing in accordance with such-and-such a law.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the Judge please ask the Prosecution whether he could show the documents that were legally sent to the bodies of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, or was everything done orally? And to a large extent, this is how the Prosecution works in cooperation with all intelligence services, and this scares witnesses and creates chaos. If you have such documents that show that you made such-and-such a request to such-and-such a witness, could you show them to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I believe that when you had contact with the local authorities, or when you have contact with them, you submit written requests to them, or is it done over the phone?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, if I could just make a couple of general observations, because there seems to be an assumption that's floating around now that whatever background checks are done is actually interfering with the Defence's ability to call witnesses. There is no proof of that, that I'm aware of, certainly. Certainly, none has been put out here. And as I indicated, I think that what we've seen so far of the Defence is to the contrary. That's number 1. Secondly, I'd be rather surprised to learn that the Defence teams, for their part, have not done their own background checking on the witnesses called by the Prosecution case in chief. It's expected, I think, and I'd be surprised if the Defence had not done the same thing themselves. In respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina, certainly because of the situation there, there is the potential for abuse, but in this respect I think it cuts both ways, and it's just the reality that the Prosecution and the Defence have to deal with when dealing with authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or Croatia, or Serbia as well. We're all dependent upon the local authorities for a variety of things, and this is one of them. But on this, the Prosecution is on an equal footing with the Defence. They can make the checks. They have to consult with the local authorities as well, and just -- and there is an equal potential for abuse when they check Prosecution witnesses. So there's no disparity here. I'm not prepared, Mr. President, to get into the specifics of the methods that we've used to conduct our background investigations or to seek the assistance of the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and nor would I expect the Defence to share that information with the Prosecution, so I'm not prepared to go into that at this time beyond saying that the Prosecution's office deals always on a formal level with the authorities of all states, including Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's been a request by Mr. Praljak as to whether there is an abuse of process. I mean, that's how I see it. I try to be rather measured. I purposely avoided getting into the discussion that Ms. Nozica got into, not because I wasn't aware of it but because I didn't want to inject politics, but such is the case in Bosnia-Herzegovina that here we have, for instance, my client, clearly a rising star within Croatian politics in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Here we have a witness who is a rising star of one of the major political parties representing the Croat nation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We have Bosnia-Herzegovina which essentially, for all intents and purposes, while on the ground it doesn't look like Iraq, the politics are nonetheless are very much the same. You have three different nations that are having the same discussions today as they were having back in 1991. That is essentially what is happening. So if, for instance, a request is made, and if one of the intelligence agencies pursues a particular request and has the ability to abuse the process, what it can essentially do is neutralise -- is neutralise certain political players back there and, of course, affect the lives of the individuals that are being tried here today. We know for a fact how intelligence agencies work. Many of them work through means of disinformation. We are not suggesting that the Prosecution has engaged in anything unlawful, but what we are saying is that perhaps when the Prosecution makes such a request, that it needs to be made in a narrow fashion. Thus far, we don't know how that request is being made; hence, Mr. Praljak indicated we would like to see if it is in writing, what exactly is being asked. Might I also say that at the beginning of this Tribunal, the life of this Tribunal back in 1993, it is a well-known fact that one of the agencies for one of the nations was working directly inside the Office of the Prosecution. That is a fact. If you also look at who has been indicted and who has not been indicted, we don't see Mr. Izetbegovic, we never saw him here, we didn't see Mr. Ganic, or Silajdzic, or others. They were investigated, they were worked, but they're not here. And so what we're worried is that these sorts of requests, benign as they may seem to be, have a very nefarious and dark nature to them, one that has far more implications for the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina politics. And all we're asking for is, one, the request be made in a very narrow fashion and, two, that such requests that have been made be provided to the Trial Chamber. Obviously, we cannot control, neither you, nor the Prosecution, what is done on that end, but we think that with some gentle prodding from the Tribunal, such requests that the Prosecution is concerned about can be made in such a way that perhaps it might be able to alleviate some of the problems. But I find it very difficult to swallow when the Prosecution says, "Well, the Defence hasn't been impacted." Yes, the witness did arrive, but, however, the witness also knew that he was intensely being investigated, and it could have gone the other way around. And how do I then come back and say, "Well, here are the reasons"? So it is having a chilling effect, albeit indirectly at this point. I'm not suggesting that I have lost any witnesses thus far, but there were other witnesses that I might have had for other reasons. So all we're asking for is one, narrow scope; two, for the Prosecution to come clean. We're entitled to this information. It also begs the question: Have they done this with their own witnesses, especially with some of the internationals that we believed worked for some of the intelligence agencies. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to say a few words without any attempt to stop the discussion. I didn't want to stop, actually, Mr. Karnavas about his final statement here. Really, I believe that now the discussion went beyond the scope of the original intentions, and it is now -- I feel that it would have been better if the statements would have been done within a kind of closed meeting, because somehow -- allowing for transparency, definitely, but some of the statements or allegations or whatever, they went beyond what I inferred was the original purpose. The original purpose was if the Prosecution asks for any kind of checking, as far as the background of the witness or witnesses concerned, and this I understand that it is an important question and one which could be raised, but now speaking about intelligence agencies, et cetera, I really believe it is now beyond our competence here, at least for the time being, and especially not within a meeting of a sitting in -- and not in a closed meeting, so I would like to ask that this issue should be closed now. We have heard the Prosecution, we have heard, of course, the Defence, and I believe that the issue could be closed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I fully appreciate what Your Honour has said. It would be quite logical for me not to have anything to add after what he has said, but I would like to say, because this may be addressed to me because I raised issues that were not referred to at the beginning, I would like us to check the transcript, because the witness said that he was being investigated by secret services, and this has prompted me to rise and to say this. So I'm referring to what I've just said. It is a danger. When official bodies are doing checkups, then there is no danger, and I think everything I said, as far as I'm concerned, can be said in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I abide by my request that it is necessary for the Prosecution to show the exact wording of the written requests addressed to the bodies of either Bosnia-Herzegovina or Croatia, what is written in them, if they are in written form, because otherwise this is for a public session. People who need to testify are trembling down there because of open attacks by various secret services. It is for the public, for the public to hear that they are free individuals, that threats made does not diminish from their ability to freely and bravely and sincerely testify in this court. If the Prosecution doesn't have those papers, let them tell us in public. As for the Prosecutor's statement and explanation, as far as I'm concerned, it is an insult for a peptogenous virus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we are going to discuss this question, whether your request should have a response from the Prosecution or not, so the Judges will deliberate on the issue this afternoon. Witness, my understanding was at the beginning that you wanted to make a statement. Is this statement linked to this or is it something else, because the Judges do not appreciate statements except at the end of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, only if the examination is over, I wanted to add two or three sentiments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but when it's over, you don't say anything except thank you to the Judges. If it is to thank the Judges, then it is okay, but if it is to say something else, there is a risk of opening a new debate, which is something that we don't want. As far as I'm concerned and on behalf of my colleagues I wish to thank you for coming to testify on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Prlic, and I wish you a safe journey home and success in the continuation of your professional and political activities. That is all I have to say about this, and I wish to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank you, too, as the President to the members of the Trial Chamber, the Defence of the accused, the Prosecution, and the accused for the possibility of saying in this courtroom my views of what the situation was like at the most difficult moments for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may leave now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to just have one brief opportunity to respond to some of the comments that were made on this last point, if in fact the Trial Chamber is going to deliberate on this any further. I think I'd like at least for the Trial Chamber to know what the Prosecution position is in respect of any further deliberations. It's our view, Mr. President, that the Office of the Prosecutor is an independent body at this Tribunal. As a party to these proceedings, it's entitled to conduct its own investigation of witnesses, as is the Defence. With respect, it's our position that it's not within the domain of the Trial Chamber to order the Prosecution to disclose or to produce its request for assistance or the work product that it makes in conducting what is legitimate background investigation, particularly where there's been no showing whatsoever of any impropriety. We've heard a lot of words from counsel and the accused himself, but there's no showing whatsoever. The witness indicated he was aware he'd been checked, but in fact he's come. I can say with absolute certainty that the Prosecution's fully aware of the pressures and the concerns that witnesses have to deal with when coming here, because there's certainly a good number of Prosecution witnesses from Bosnia-Herzegovina, or Croatia, or internationals as well who to this day carry a lot of fear of these gentlemen and the HVO and the repercussions of their coming here, and they also know the situation that exists politically down in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So these are risks that all the witnesses run. And there are witnesses that were not heard during the Prosecution case because of these concerns, and that may be true of the Defence as well. But on this, we're on equal footing. But in any event, Mr. President, I think I just wanted to make that clear that -- what the Prosecution position is on this issue, and I appreciate you giving me the opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with your leave, I did stand earlier and sat down to my chair again when His Honour Judge Prandler was making his remarks and giving guidance to the Trial Chamber. I do agree, in part, with what my learned friend has just said. Matters are, to some degree, speculative until there is a showing that the administration of justice has been thwarted or otherwise imperiled, but I don't accept for one moment that the overall superintendence of the Trial Chamber takes a back seat under the alter of prosecutorial independence. Of course, independence of the Prosecution is there. They are, as a separate organ of the Court, the Prosecutor is independent, but that does not give any Prosecutor cart blanche to do whatever they want. We know from proceedings in this court, in this Tribunal, as well as of course the Lubanga proceedings and the stay there, that a trial chamber does have its obligation to police the system so as to ensure that the Statute and the Rules are fully enforced. Now, this is academic to some degree, but of course if it is shown that an action of the Prosecutor -- if it's shown that an action of a Prosecutor has a chilling effect so as to bring the administration of justice into disrepute or to otherwise obstruct the truth-finding exercise, that is the highest and most fundamental responsibility for which this Tribunal was established. Of course, prosecutorial independence cannot trump Your Honours' oath of office to ensure justice in this case. I think the issue became somewhat emotive, as my learned leader mentioned, because of the use of intelligence services. For my part, I have no problem for one moment for the Prosecution contacting the police services of any state to make a background check of any witness. That's normal. I don't see anything objectionable in that at all. Police services, of course, have records based upon evidence of criminality, and often evidence of a conviction. Counsel even, in some courts, in the ICC, have to disclose if they have previous convictions before they got on the list. I have no problem with that. But intelligence services, of course, have been a perennial problem in many systems about having oversight and superintendence. They deal not just in fact, but in speculation, innuendo, and other aspects, and I think in part one of the reasons why this became a live issue, and it may be completely speculative, it may have been something that the witness believed which has not been proved, but it's because of the mention of intelligence services, in highly partisan and highly politicised environments, as opposed to the legitimate police enforcement mechanisms of the state, which are the police services, and I think that is a matter that perhaps, whilst this matter is being raised now, that the Prosecution may consider as a matter of their own internal policies. I think there is a real difference between the two. Your Honour, those are my remarks in response, but if there is a showing, if there is a showing, of course, my primary submission must be that there is nothing that would enable Your Honours or persuade Your Honours to step aside and abdicate your fundamental responsibility to ensure justice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Praljak, you wanted to intervene?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will take a bit of time, but in view of the sensitivity of the issue, could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the question raised regarding intelligence services is closed, because the Judges will discuss it and deliberate about it. I give you the floor now for the purpose of your intervention. You want us to go into private session, fine, we'll go into private session. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
